analysis.one_liner: Imposes a small tax on Wall Street trades of stocks, bonds, and derivatives to fund public programs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2021 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a small tax on every purchase of a stock, bond, partnership interest, or derivative that happens in the United States or involves a U.S. party: half a percent on stocks, a tenth of a percent on bonds, and a tiny fraction on derivatives. Exchanges, brokers, or traders would pay it, and households making under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples) would get their money back through a tax credit. The bill's findings say the revenue could fund college, child care, infrastructure, health care, and climate programs, and that the tax would mainly hit high-frequency trading, which makes up a large share of market volume. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and died there; it never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income households, who would be made whole through the tax credit; retirees and mutual fund holders, who the bill says would see a negligible cost; and any programs funded by the new revenue, such as college, child care, infrastructure, health care, and climate efforts.

how_it_helps.text: Charges a 0.5% tax on stock transfers, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives, paid by exchanges, brokers, or the traders themselves [S3].
Refunds the tax in full to individuals with incomes up to $50,000 ($75,000 joint) through a tax credit, so most ordinary investors would pay nothing net [S3].

The bill's findings state the revenue could fund free college, child care, Social Security, infrastructure, Medicare and Medicaid expansion, housing assistance, and climate programs, and that economists estimate such a tax could raise hundreds of billions annually [S3].
The findings say a transactions tax would curb high-frequency trading, which the bill says may be as much as 70% of market volume and contributes to price volatility [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms and high-frequency traders, who would pay the tax on each transaction; the bill also allows new penalties for failing to report covered transactions, and it expects avoidance attempts through foreign intermediaries, which is why it directs regulators to write anti-avoidance rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large trading firms and hedge funds

drawbacks.text: Trading costs could be passed on to ordinary investors through fund managers and retirement accounts, and the bill's own findings acknowledge the tax targets a market where high-frequency trading is a large share of volume, so the market itself would restructure around the tax [S3].

The tax could be avoided by routing trades through foreign facilities or non-U.S. parties, which the bill anticipates by directing the Treasury Secretary to write regulations preventing avoidance, but no such rules exist yet, so revenue and burden-shifting are uncertain [S3].

The bill does not actually designate the revenue to specific programs; its findings list possible uses but the tax itself only adds revenue to the general treasury, so whether it funds any of the listed priorities depends on later appropriations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is a new revenue stream whose burden falls mostly on high-volume trading, with a full refund protecting small investors. The main cost is uncertainty: real-world financial transaction taxes have sometimes raised less revenue than projected and shifted costs onto everyday investors through wider trading spreads, and this bill does not guarantee any of the listed program spending. The design is serious about protecting low-income households but leaves the use of the money and the anti-avoidance rules to later decisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and no further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 21, 2021 by Sen. Sanders with Sen. Gillibrand [S1].
Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No hearings, markups, amendments, votes, or floor action are recorded for the bill in the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wall Street trading firms and high-volume traders avoided a new tax on every stock, bond, and derivative trade, and the Finance Committee's inaction kept the bill from ever being debated.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on April 21, 2021.

for.name: Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Sanders at introduction.

for.name: 2 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Two Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors; no other Democrats joined before the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No one opposed the bill on the record because it never got a hearing or vote; support was limited to Sanders, Gillibrand, and two other Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican backing.

industries.note: The bill would tax every covered trade at rates aimed at high-frequency trading and derivatives, the highest-volume corners of the market. Industry lobbyists have historically opposed such taxes, arguing they raise trading costs and push activity offshore.

industries.industry: Stock, bond, and derivatives exchanges and brokers
industries.note: Exchanges and brokers are made the collectors of the tax, adding compliance obligations and potentially reducing trading volume they profit from. Their costs could be passed to customers.

The bill assumes a negligible impact on average investors, and a tax credit refunds the tax for households under $50,000 ($75,000 joint), but some pass-through of trading costs to fund holders is possible.
